Ghent
gent
n. (the great Flemish town whose Calvinist republic of 1577 suppressed the mass by force and lost the south for the Reformation)
Dutch Gent, French Gand, from the Celtic condate, a confluence, for the meeting of the Lys and the Scheldt.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ghent was the largest town of Flanders and the most turbulent, with a long tradition of guild risings against its counts, and in the revolt against Spain it put a Calvinist government in power and used it hard. The Pacification of Ghent in November 1576 had united the provinces, Catholic and Protestant together, against the Spanish soldiery on the understanding that each province would keep its own religion. Ghent broke that understanding. From 1577 Jan van Hembyze and Francois van Ryhove governed the town as a Calvinist republic, suppressed the mass, imprisoned the bishop, seized church property, forced the surrounding Flemish towns into the same settlement, and treated the Catholic nobility of the revolt as enemies. The southern provinces answered with the Union of Arras in January 1579; William of Orange came in person to Ghent to restrain Hembyze and failed; and Parma took the town in 1584. The dictionary enters Ghent as a judgement against our own side. Flanders was lost to the Reformation, and the loss was not only Spain's work: the Reformed party in Ghent had the mass abolished by magistrates and soldiers rather than preached down, and the provinces that might have gone with them went to the king instead.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a guild as a society or corporation; pacification as the act of making peace; to suppress as to crush or put an end to; and sedition as a commotion in a state.

expand to see more

GUILD, n. A society, fraternity or corporation, associated for some common purpose, as of trade.

PACIFICATION, n. The act of making peace between parties at variance; the act of appeasing wrath.

SUPPRESS, v. To crush; to subdue; to put an end to; to overpower and destroy.

SEDITION, n. A factious commotion of the people; a tumultuous assembly of men rising in opposition to law or the administration.

ZEAL, n. Passionate ardor in the pursuit of any thing; in general, zeal is an eagerness of desire to accomplish an object.

Modern Corruption

Great Flemish town whose Calvinist republic of 1577 suppressed the mass by force, provoked the Union of Arras, and fell to Parma in 1584.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is our own, and Ghent is where it is clearest. Hembyze's government had zeal, and the apostle's description of a zeal that misses its mark fits it exactly: “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2). The mass is a corruption of the Lord's Supper and the dictionary says so without qualification; it was not Ghent's magistrates' business to end it by imprisoning a bishop and coercing neighbouring towns, and the direct consequence was that the Catholic nobility of the revolt signed with Spain and ten provinces were lost.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the means by which the church is actually built, which is not the magistrate's arm. “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) was spoken over a building project, and “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal” (2Co 10:4) is the apostolic rule for the same work. The temper is judged too, for “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20), and the wrath in Ghent was on the Reformed side as well as the Spanish.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek zelos (G2205), zeal, fervour; Greek sarkikos (G4559), carnal; Hebrew ruach (H7307), spirit, breath.

expand to see more

Greek zelos (G2205) — zeal, fervour, heat of spirit; “they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Greek epignosis (G1922) — full knowledge, discernment; “but not according to knowledge”, Romans 10:2.

Greek sarkikos (G4559) — fleshly, carnal; “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal”, 2 Corinthians 10:4.

Greek orge (G3709) — wrath, settled anger; “the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God”, James 1:20.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; “but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts”, Zechariah 4:6.

Usage

"“they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2) — Hembyze's Calvinist republic, 1577 to 1584."

"“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6) — the mass abolished by magistrates and soldiers."

"“the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God” (Jam 1:20) — neighbouring Flemish towns coerced into the settlement."
